screening_decisions.reason: This is a randomised controlled trial in women with stress urinary incontinence (SUI), matching the population requirement. One trial arm received pelvic floor muscle exercises (PFMT) via digital palpation, another via biofeedback (both are PFMT), and the third arm received no treatment, serving as an inactive control. Thus, the study includes a PFMT arm and a no-treatment control arm, meeting the selection criteria for PFMT versus inactive control.

This is an RCT of a mobile app delivering PFMT versus postponed treatment (inactive control) in women with stress urinary incontinence. The intervention group performed pelvic floor muscle training; the control group received no treatment during the study. The study fully meets the review's inclusion criteria for population (women with SUI), intervention (PFMT), comparator (inactive control), and study design (RCT).

The study is a randomized controlled trial (RCT) among postmenopausal women with stress urinary incontinence (SUI), matching the required population (women with SUI, UUI, or MUI). It includes an arm receiving pelvic floor muscle exercises (PFME, a form of PFMT) and a control arm that was assessed only at baseline and after 1 month, implying no active treatment. This meets the criterion of having one arm with PFMT and another arm as a no-treatment or inactive control. Therefore, the study fulfills all inclusion criteria for the review on PFMT versus no treatment/inactive controls for urinary incontinence in women.

The study compares biofeedback-assisted behavioral treatment with drug treatment and placebo, not pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT). The review inclusion criteria require that one arm of the trial includes PFMT. The abstract does not mention PFMT or pelvic floor muscle exercises; behavioral treatment for urge incontinence may consist of bladder training and urge suppression strategies rather than PFMT. Therefore, the study does not meet the intervention criterion.
RCT in women with SUI; one arm received pelvic muscle exercise (PFMT) and another was a control group (inactive treatment). All criteria satisfied.

The study is a single-blind, stratified randomized controlled trial enrolling women with urodynamically proven genuine stress incontinence, which falls under SUI. It includes an arm of pelvic floor exercises (PFMT) and a no-treatment control arm (untreated control group). Thus, it meets all selection criteria: RCT, population with SUI, one arm PFMT, another arm no treatment (inactive control). There are additional active comparator arms (electrical stimulation, vaginal cones) but the presence of the no-treatment control satisfies the protocol.

The study is a randomized controlled trial (participants distributed randomly) in women with stress urinary incontinence (SUI). It compares pelvic floor muscle exercises (perineal exercises) — which constitute PFMT — to a control group that likely received no active treatment (inactive control), as the abstract mentions both groups had assessments but only the experimental group received 16 sessions of exercises. Thus it meets all selection criteria: population (women with SUI), intervention (PFMT), comparison (no treatment/inactive control), and study design (randomized). This warrants inclusion for full-text review.

This is a randomised controlled trial (randomly selected) in women with urodynamic stress urinary incontinence (SUI, based on urodynamics). One arm of the trial includes pelvic floor exercises (PFMT) and another arm is no active treatment (untreated control), which is an inactive control treatment. The study meets all the selection criteria: RCT design, women with SUI, PFMT in one arm, and an inactive control (no treatment) in another. The presence of additional active comparator arms (electrical stimulation, vaginal cones) does not affect eligibility.

The study is a randomized controlled trial that enrolled 130 women with stress and mixed urinary incontinence (SUI/MUI), meeting the population criterion. One arm per formed a 12‑week home‑based pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) programme, exactly the required intervention. The comparator is referred to only as 'control group' without any mention of active treatment; it is interpreted as a no‑treatment or inactive control, satisfying the comparator criterion. The study design is a prospective RCT. Following the conservative guideline, any uncertainty about the control condition justifies inclusion.

The study is a randomized controlled trial in women with urinary incontinence. The intervention, a behavioral modification program (BMP), likely includes pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) because the abstract reports significant improvements in pelvic floor muscle strength (pressure, displacement, duration) in the treatment group. The control arm received no treatment. Thus, one arm arguably included PFMT, meeting the selection criteria. Include for full-text review to confirm the precise content of BMP.

The study is a randomized controlled trial comparing two forms of physical therapy (medical gymnastics and perineal electrical stimulation) for female stress incontinence. There is no mention of a no-treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control arm, which is a necessary comparator as per the selection criteria. Therefore, it does not meet the comparison criterion.

The study is a randomized controlled trial enrolling women with stress urinary incontinence (SUI). The intervention includes pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) directed at enhancing PFMs, meeting the PFMT arm requirement. The control arm is described simply as 'control' without mention of an active treatment; in a crossover design, this typically represents an initial no-treatment or waiting-list condition, which qualifies as an inactive control. Thus, the study fulfills the criteria: RCT in women with SUI, one arm PFMT, the other an inactive control. Following conservative screening guidelines (include when uncertain), this study should proceed.

The study does not specify that the exercise intervention includes pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT). The exercise program led to improvements in overall muscle strength and walking speed, which are not typical outcomes of PFMT. Because the review inclusion criteria require an arm with PFMT, and this trial lacks a clearly identifiable PFMT arm, it should be excluded. The education group serves as an inactive control, but the active treatment is not PFMT.

The intervention is described as 'multidimensional exercise treatment' with no explicit component of pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT). The review requires one trial arm to include PFMT. Without evidence that PFMT was part of the intervention, this study does not meet the inclusion criteria.

RCT in women with stress, urge, or mixed UI; intervention arm includes PFMT (with manual palpation/feedback); control arm (advice + pamphlet) is an inactive control (minimal information only, no therapeutic PFMT component). Meets all inclusion criteria. Conservative inclusion applied due to borderline control type.

The study is a randomized controlled trial enrolling women with stress urinary incontinence (SUI). The intervention group receives pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) and the control group receives no treatment, which qualifies as an inactive control. The study thus satisfies all selection criteria: randomized or quasi-randomized design, population with SUI, one arm with PFMT, and a no-treatment control arm. Outcome measures include relevant clinical and morphological outcomes.

This is a prospective, randomised, single-blind controlled trial in women with stress urinary incontinence (SUI). The intervention arm is taught 'The Knack', which is a timed pelvic floor muscle contraction – a technique that falls directly under the umbrella of pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT). The control arm is a wait-list group, which constitutes an inactive control (no treatment during the comparison period). Therefore the study satisfies all key selection criteria: randomised design, women with SUI, one arm receiving PFMT, and the other an inactive control.

Randomized controlled pilot study (RCT) in women with stress urinary incontinence (SUI). Two arms involved pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) – group and individual sessions – and a third arm was a no-treatment control group. Thus, the study meets all inclusion criteria: RCT design, female population with SUI, PFMT intervention in at least one arm, and an inactive (no treatment) control arm.

This is a randomised controlled pilot trial in women with mixed urinary incontinence (MUI). Participants were randomly assigned to TCM acupuncture, PFMT, or waiting list control. One arm is PFMT (physiotherapy), and another arm is waiting list (inactive control). Thus, it meets the criteria: RCT in women with MUI (based on symptoms), one arm PFMT, another arm inactive control. Even though it is a pilot study, the design satisfies eligibility. Include.

Randomized controlled trial in women with urinary incontinence. The intervention is 'physical therapy for UI (12 weekly sessions)', which typically includes pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT). The comparator is 'osteoporosis education', an inactive control for UI. Study design, population, and comparator meet inclusion criteria. Although PFMT is not explicitly named in the abstract, the standard physical therapy for UI in women almost always incorporates PFMT; under the conservative screening guideline, this uncertainty warrants inclusion.

The study includes an arm with pelvic muscle exercises (PFMT) and a control group. Although the abstract does not specify the nature of the control group, it likely is no treatment or inactive control, meeting the review criteria of comparing PFMT to an inactive control. Additionally, the population is women with urinary incontinence. Therefore, it meets the inclusion criteria. Confidence: medium due to lack of explicit control type description.

The study is a randomized controlled trial in women with stress urinary incontinence (SUI). The interventions include kinesitherapy (which likely consists of pelvic floor muscle training) versus a control group. One arm (G2: kinesitherapy alone) provides pelvic floor muscle training compared to a control group (G3), which aligns with the required comparison of PFMT vs inactive control. Although the abstract does not explicitly state PFMT, kinesitherapy for pelvic floor commonly includes pelvic floor muscle exercises, and the focus on muscle contraction supports this interpretation. Given the conservative inclusion guideline, this study should be included.

The study randomly allocated female athletes with urinary leakage (likely stress urinary incontinence, as concluded) to a pelvic floor muscle training program (PFMRP) or a pamphlet-only control (inactive control). It meets the criteria: population - women with probable stress urinary incontinence; intervention - PFMT; comparator - inactive control (pamphlet); design - randomised controlled trial. Uncertainties about formal SUI diagnosis are resolved conservatively by inclusion.

The study is a randomized controlled trial in women with stress urinary incontinence (SUI). It includes an arm receiving pelvic floor exercises (PFMT) and an inactive control group. This meets the selection criteria: randomized trial in women with SUI, with PFMT versus inactive control.

The study is a randomized controlled trial that assigned 66 women with genuine stress incontinence (i.e., SUI) to either pelvic floor exercises (PFMT) or a no‑treatment control group. This satisfies the review’s selection criteria: it is an RCT (random assignment), the population consists of women with SUI based on symptoms, the intervention arm uses PFMT, and the comparator is an inactive control (no therapy). Therefore, the study clearly meets all requirements for inclusion.

This study is a parallel-group randomized clinical trial (RCT) that evaluates the effectiveness of pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) in women diagnosed with stress or mixed urinary incontinence (SUI/MUI). It meets all selection criteria: (1) study design is a randomized controlled trial; (2) population consists of women with SUI or MUI based on symptoms, recruited from urology clinics; (3) intervention arm includes PFMT with instructed exercises and follow-up; (4) control arm is an untreated (no treatment) group, which is an inactive control. Outcomes include incontinence episodes (bladder diary), pad test, quality of life, and PFM strength. Therefore, the study satisfies the criteria for inclusion.

The study does not meet the selection criteria for three reasons. (1) Population: the inclusion criteria require women with stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence (SUI, UUI, MUI) based on symptoms, signs, or urodynamics. The study enrolls 'all consecutive patients consulting their general practitioner within 1 year for urinary incontinence', which likely includes both men and women, and does not restrict by UI subtype (could include overflow, functional, or other types). (2) Intervention: the trial compares the involvement of a nurse specialist in primary care versus usual care, not PFMT versus an inactive control. Although 'usual care' may contain PFMT, the intervention itself is the nurse practitioner involvement, not PFMT as a standalone arm. The protocol explicitly requires one arm to be PFMT. (3) Comparison: the control is usual care, not a no-treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control treatment. 'Usual care' may include active treatments, so it is not an inactive control. For these reasons, the study is clearly ineligible for this Cochrane Review update.

The study is a randomized controlled trial comparing nurse specialist care to usual GP care for urinary incontinence. It does not involve pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), which is a core eligibility criterion. The intervention arm must include PFMT, and the control arm must be no treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control. Here both arms are active care models. Additionally, the population is not clearly limited to women (the abstract refers only to 'patients') and does not specify stress, urgency, or mixed UI subtypes. Therefore, it fails to meet the selection criteria on multiple levels.

The study is a RCT in women with urge/mixed incontinence, including PFMT in multiple arms. However, the control group received a self-help booklet that constituted an active behavioral treatment, not a no‑treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control as required by the review criteria. Therefore, the comparison condition is not met.

The study is a feasibility study (not a randomised or quasi‑randomised controlled trial). No random allocation was used; participants volunteered and groups were formed by site, with an education‑only control that is not an inactive control arm as required by the protocol. Therefore it does not meet the fundamental study design criterion.

The study compares two active pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) interventions (supervised vs unsupervised) in women with stress urinary incontinence. Both arms involve PFMT, and there is no arm receiving no treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control treatment. Therefore, it does not meet the protocol requirement that one arm must be an inactive control.

The study is a randomized controlled trial in women with stress UI, and the intervention (stabilization exercises focusing on pelvic floor muscle) likely qualifies as PFMT. However, the control group received 'routine physiotherapy modalities and regular exercises', which is an active treatment, not a no-treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control as required by the review. Therefore, the study does not meet the selection criteria.

The study compares behavioral training (which likely includes PFMT) with or without PFES, and a self-help booklet control. The control arm ('self-administered behavioral treatment using a self-help booklet') is an active intervention, not a no treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control as required by the review criteria. Therefore, the study does not meet the selection criteria for control comparisons.

The study is a randomized controlled trial that specifically enrolled women with urinary incontinence (UI). Although the abstract does not specify the type of UI, it is reasonable to assume that participants include those with stress, urgency, or mixed UI, as defined in the review criteria. The intervention arm included Kegel's exercises, which constitute pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT). The control group is described only as 'control group'; the abstract does not provide enough detail to determine whether it was an active treatment. At the title/abstract screening stage, a conservative approach dictates inclusion when uncertainty exists about the control condition. Further evaluation at full-text stage can clarify the nature of the control arm. Therefore, the study meets the broad criteria for inclusion.

The study's intervention is 'behavioral therapy', not the pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) specified in the review's selection criteria. The review requires one arm to include PFMT; this study compares a behavioral therapy arm to a no-therapy control, so it does not meet the intervention requirement. Although it is a randomized controlled trial in women with urinary incontinence, the intervention is not the targeted treatment.

This is an economic evaluation alongside a randomized controlled trial that compares two active pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) delivery methods (internet‐based vs postal). Although the analysis includes a no‐treatment option, that comparator is based on unchanged baseline data and was not a randomized arm of the trial. The selection criteria require a trial arm with no treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control treatment; this study compares two active PFMT arms only, so it does not meet the criteria.

The study compares two active treatment arms (Internet-based PFMT program vs. postal-based PFMT program). Both arms include pelvic floor muscle training, but the review protocol requires that the comparator arm be a no treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control treatment. The postal arm is an active PFMT program, not an inactive control, so the study does not meet the inclusion criteria.

The study is a randomized controlled trial in women with stress urinary incontinence, but it compares two active pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) delivery methods (internet-based vs postal). There is no no-treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control arm. Therefore, it does not meet the selection criterion that requires a control arm of no treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control treatment.

The study is a randomized controlled trial enrolling women with stress urinary incontinence (SUI), satisfying the population criterion. The intervention group performs pelvic floor muscle (PFM) co-contraction exercises, thus PFMT is included as a component of the intervention, meeting the intervention criterion. The control group is not described in detail but is likely an inactive control (no treatment or usual care); in the absence of contrary information, it is conservatively assumed to meet the comparator criterion of no active treatment. Therefore, the study meets all inclusion criteria.

The study does not meet the intervention criterion: one arm of the trial must include pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT). The intervention described is a combination of customized behavioral UI treatments plus 150 minutes of weekly walking and twice-weekly strength training classes—none of which constitute PFMT. PFMT involves specific exercises targeting the pelvic floor muscles, not general physical activity or behavioral strategies. Although the trial is a randomized controlled trial in women with UI and a control arm, the active arm lacks PFMT, so it fails the selection criteria. Exclusion is clear-cut.

The study includes gynecologic cancer survivors with pelvic floor dysfunction, not specifically women with stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence. The review requires a population with SUI, UUI, or MUI based on symptoms, signs, or urodynamics. Since the abstract does not state that participants had urinary incontinence, it does not meet the population criterion.

The study is a psychometric validation of the ICIQ questionnaire, not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. It does not compare pelvic floor muscle training to a no-treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control arm. Therefore, it clearly fails the study design requirement.

This study is a systematic review of randomized clinical trials, not itself a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. The selection criteria require primary RCTs or quasi-RCTs; systematic reviews are not eligible.

The study is a systematic review of randomized clinical trials, not itself a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. The selection criteria specify that included studies must be randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials. As a systematic review, this study does not meet the required study design.

The study is a methodological paper on reporting standards for nonpharmacologic trials. It does not present a randomized or quasi-randomised controlled trial. It does not include women with stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence, nor does it compare pelvic floor muscle training to a control condition. Therefore, it does not meet any of the inclusion criteria.

The study is a narrative review or commentary discussing the psychological impact of urinary incontinence in both men and women. It does not describe a randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trial design. There is no mention of pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) as an intervention, nor any comparison with a no treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control arm. Therefore, it fails to meet the core selection criteria requiring a trial of PFMT versus inactive control in women with stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence.

The study is a psychometric validation of a quality-of-life questionnaire (I-QOL) and not a randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trial. It does not assess any intervention, particularly pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT). There is no mention of an active treatment arm involving PFMT or a control arm with no treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control. The study does not meet the inclusion criteria for study design.

The study is not a randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trial. It is a reproducibility study that develops and tests two measurement instruments without any comparison of pelvic floor muscle training versus a control group. Therefore, it does not meet the inclusion criteria for trial design or intervention.

This study is not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. It is an observational cross-sectional study using dynamic MRI to describe pelvic floor muscle movement during contraction and straining in women with and without stress incontinence. There is no intervention arm of pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) and no comparison with a no treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control treatment. Therefore, it does not meet the inclusion criteria for type of study design or intervention/comparator.

The study is not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. It is a narrative review discussing theoretical mechanisms behind the effectiveness of PFM training, citing existing RCTs and anatomical studies. It does not meet the study design requirement of the selection criteria.

The study is a consensus terminology report, not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. The selection criteria require RCTs or quasi-RCTs in women with stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence comparing pelvic floor muscle training with an inactive control. This study does not report original trial data and thus cannot meet the study design criterion. The population described (female pelvic floor dysfunction) may include UI, but the absence of a controlled trial design makes it ineligible. Even a conservative approach would not include this report as it does not present any comparative effectiveness data.

The study is a secondary analysis of a cross-sectional internet survey (EpiLUTS), not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. It does not include any intervention arm, and specifically no arm of pelvic floor muscle training. Additionally, it includes both men and women, whereas the review criteria specify women with SUI, UUI, or MUI. Therefore, it clearly does not meet the eligibility criteria.

The study is a review chapter on pharmacology of the lower urinary tract. It does not describe a randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trial, does not involve women with SUI, UUI, or MUI as a trial population, and does not include pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) as an intervention. There is no comparison to a no treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control arm. Therefore, it clearly fails all components of the selection criteria. Exclusion is certain with high confidence.

The study is a narrative review aiming to review evidence and discuss literature, not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. It does not meet the study design criterion of being an RCT or quasi-RCT. Although it discusses RCTs, it is itself a review article and therefore excluded.

The study is about functional electrical stimulation (FES) applied to the anal sphincter to inhibit detrusor activity, not about pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT). The review specifically requires one arm of the trial to include PFMT, and the other arm to be a control (no treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive). This study does not involve PFMT. Additionally, the abstract does not specify that the population consists of women with stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence; it discusses incontinence in the context of neurogenic bladder hyperreflexia, which may include both sexes. Therefore, it fails both the intervention and population criteria.

The study population consists of healthy women without urinary incontinence, failing to meet the criterion that participants must have stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence. Additionally, the study is not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial with a pelvic floor muscle training arm versus an inactive control; it is a secondary analysis of pelvic muscle resting pressures during a graded exercise program without a comparison group, and no assessment of incontinence outcomes.

The study is a methodological guideline paper on constructing Summary of Findings tables for systematic reviews. It is not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial, does not include women with any type of urinary incontinence, and does not compare pelvic floor muscle training against no treatment or inactive control. Hence, it clearly fails to meet the inclusion criteria of the review.

This study is a methodological guidance document on presenting continuous outcomes in GRADE summary of findings tables. It is not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial, does not involve women with stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence, and does not include an intervention arm of pelvic floor muscle training. Therefore, it does not meet any of the inclusion criteria (population, intervention, comparison, study design).

This study is a cross-sectional epidemiological survey aiming to estimate prevalence of urinary incontinence, not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. There is no intervention (PFMT) and no control arm. Therefore it clearly fails to meet the study design criterion of RCT or quasi-RCT.

The study is a consensus terminology report for female pelvic floor dysfunction, not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. It does not have a PFMT intervention arm or an inactive control arm, thus failing the study design requirement.

The study is a methodological analysis of intervention quality in systematic reviews, not a randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trial. It does not investigate PFMT, nor does it include women with stress, urgency or mixed urinary incontinence. Therefore, it clearly fails the selection criteria (study design and population).

The study is a cross-sectional, observational study that assesses quality of life using the Sickness Impact Profile in women with urinary incontinence (UI). It does not involve any randomized or quasi-randomized allocation to intervention groups. There is no pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) arm and no inactive control arm (no treatment, placebo, sham). Therefore, it does not meet the required study design (RCT or q-RCT) nor the intervention criteria (PFMT vs. inactive control).
The study is a systematic review and economic modelling, not a randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trial. The selection criteria require original trials, not secondary research syntheses.

The study is a questionnaire development and psychometric validation study, not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. It does not compare PFMT against a no-treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control arm. Therefore, it does not meet the review's inclusion criteria for study design or intervention.

This is a cross-sectional willingness-to-pay survey, not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. It does not compare pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) to any control (no treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control). The selection criteria require a trial design with one arm including PFMT and another arm as a control; this study lacks both an intervention and a comparator arm. Thus, it clearly does not meet the eligibility criteria.

The study is a cross-sectional analysis using multivariate logistic regression, not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. It does not compare pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) to a control; it investigates the association between urinary incontinence and self-rated health. Therefore, it fails to meet the study design and intervention criteria.

This study is a questionnaire development and validation study, not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. It does not compare pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) to a no treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control arm. Therefore, it does not meet the selection criteria for study design and intervention.

The study is a validation study for a psychosocial scale (YIPS) and does not assess the efficacy of pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT). The intervention is a behavioral/educational intervention, not PFMT as required. The control arm is not specified, but even if it were an inactive control, the intervention does not match the PFMT criterion. The population, while women with urinary incontinence, is not limited to stress, urgency, or mixed UI based on symptoms, signs, or urodynamics; it is a general incontinence diagnosis. Therefore, the study does not meet the inclusion criteria for this review.

The study is not a randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trial. It is a qualitative content validity study of a patient-reported outcome questionnaire. It does not have an intervention arm of pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) and does not have a no treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control arm. Furthermore, the study includes men, whereas the review requires studies in women. Therefore, it clearly does not meet the selection criteria.

This study is a methodological meta-research article examining how trial quality influences pooled effect estimates in meta-analyses, not a randomized controlled trial evaluating pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) in women with urinary incontinence. The study population is not women with SUI, UUI, or MUI, and no PFMT intervention or inactive control is investigated. It does not meet any inclusion criteria of the review.

The study is a reporting guideline for RCTs (CONSORT statement), not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial of pelvic floor muscle training for urinary incontinence in women. It does not enroll women with stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence, nor does it compare PFMT to a no-treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control arm. Therefore, it fails all the PICO and study design elements of the selection criteria.

This study is a cross-sectional survey assessing the bothersomeness and quality of life impact of urinary incontinence. It is not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial, and does not compare pelvic floor muscle training to any control. Therefore it does not meet the eligibility criteria of being an RCT/quasi-RCT with PFMT versus inactive control.

This study aims only to describe normal pelvic floor muscle characteristics in healthy, continent, nulliparous women. It is a small observational study (10 volunteers) with no comparison group and no intervention. The population does not meet the criterion of women with stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence (the participants were healthy and continent). Moreover, the study design is not a randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trial, and neither arm includes pelvic floor muscle training versus an inactive control. Therefore, it fails all key eligibility criteria.

### 1. Task outcome (short version):
EXCLUDE

### 2. Task outcome (extremely detailed version):
This study is excluded because it does not meet the inclusion criteria for study design and intervention.
The review requires randomised or quasi‑randomised controlled trials in women with stress, urgency, or mixed
urinary incontinence, where one arm receives pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) and another arm receives
no treatment, placebo, sham, or another inactive control. The current study is a methodological study that
develops and validates a severity index for urinary incontinence, comparing it against 48‑hour pad‑weighing
tests. It is not a clinical trial, involves no randomisation, and does not evaluate PFMT or any other
intervention. Therefore, it fails on multiple criteria: not an RCT/quasi‑RCT, no PFMT arm, and no inactive
control arm. It is clearly ineligible.

### 3. Additional context (if relevant):
None.

The study is an observational cross-sectional study comparing sexual function between incontinent and continent women, with no intervention involving PFMT. It does not meet the criteria for a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial with PFMT versus inactive control.

The study is a prospective cohort study, not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. It does not compare pelvic floor muscle training against a no treatment or inactive control. The population includes both men and women (community-dwelling incontinent adults), whereas the review requires women with stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence. Therefore, it does not meet the inclusion criteria.

This study describes the development and validation of short-form versions of the Incontinence Impact Questionnaire (IIQ) and Urogenital Distress Inventory (UDI) to assess quality of life and symptom distress in women with urinary incontinence. It is not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial, and it does not include any treatment arms (PFMT or inactive control). Therefore it does not meet the selection criteria, which require a trial design comparing PFMT to a no-treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control in women with stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence.

The study is a measurement development and validation study for a quality of life questionnaire (I-QOL) in urinary incontinence. It is not a randomized or quasi-randomised controlled trial, nor does it compare pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) to an inactive control. Thus, it does not meet the study design inclusion criteria.

The study is a psychometric validation of a quality of life scale in psoriasis patients. It does not involve women with stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence; does not include pelvic floor muscle training as an intervention; and is not a randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trial comparing PFMT to an inactive control. Therefore it fails to meet multiple eligibility criteria (population, intervention, study design).

The study is a secondary analysis of data from double-blind, placebo-controlled trials evaluating duloxetine (a pharmacological treatment) for stress urinary incontinence. There is no pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) arm. The selection criteria require one arm of the trial to include PFMT and another arm to be a no treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control. This study does not involve PFMT at all, and therefore clearly does not meet the inclusion criteria.

The study is about development and validation of a self-assessment scale for anxiety and depression in hospital outpatients. It is not a randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trial, does not involve women with stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence, and does not evaluate pelvic floor muscle training versus no treatment or an inactive control. Therefore it does not meet any of the selection criteria.

The study is a randomized controlled trial in women with stress urinary incontinence (SUI), comparing pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) to a control group. The abstract does not explicitly describe the control condition, but it is plausible that the control group received no treatment or an inactive intervention (common in PFMT trials). As the review accepts no treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive controls, and given the conservative inclusion principle, this study meets the design criteria at this stage. The presence of SUI, randomization, and PFMT arm satisfy the other criteria.

This is a randomized controlled trial in women with stress urinary incontinence (SUI). One trial arm (GE) received perineal exercises (pelvic floor muscle training, PFMT) alone, and another arm (GC) was a control group that appears to be a no-treatment or other inactive control. Therefore, the study meets the review's inclusion criteria: it is a randomized trial in women with SUI, including a PFMT arm and an inactive control comparator.

The study is a randomized controlled trial evaluating acupressure for women with urodynamic stress incontinence. While the population matches the criteria (women with SUI based on urodynamics) and the control arms include sham and usual care, none of the arms involves pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT). The review requires that at least one arm includes PFMT; therefore, this study does not meet the selection criteria.

The study is a randomized trial in women with SUI, which meets the population and design criteria. However, the trial compares a supervised pelvic floor exercise program (SEP) added to a home prescribed exercise program (HEP) versus HEP alone. Both arms involve active pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT); the control arm is not a no treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control. This violates the requirement that one arm must be an inactive control treatment arm. Therefore, the study does not meet the selection criteria.

The study is a randomized controlled trial in women with stress urinary incontinence (SUI). It includes an arm that received pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) alone and another arm that received no active treatment (imitation PFMT plus placebo), which satisfies the criteria of PFMT versus no treatment or an inactive control. The population is women with SUI, consistent with the review's inclusion population. Therefore, the study meets all selection criteria.

The study is a qualitative interview study exploring participants' experiences of two PFMT delivery modes (Internet-based vs postal), not a randomized or quasi-randomised controlled trial. The abstract indicates it is a qualitative substudy using grounded theory, not a trial comparing PFMT to an inactive control. Therefore, it does not satisfy the study design criterion of a randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trial.

The study is not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. It is a secondary analysis of a cohort of women with SUI who all received PFMT delivered via internet or brochure, and aims to identify predictors of long-term success. There is no comparison arm of no treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control. Therefore, the study design does not meet the selection criteria requiring one arm PFMT and another arm an inactive control. The intervention (PFMT) is present, but the absence of an eligible control arm makes this study clearly ineligible.

The study is a systematic review, not a randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trial, thus failing the study design criterion. Additionally, the comparison is PFMT added to another active treatment versus the same active treatment alone, not against a no treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control arm as required. Therefore it clearly does not meet the selection criteria.

The article is a review/overview of exercise science for pelvic floor muscle training for SUI. It compiled and summarized 16 previous studies; it is not itself a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. The selection criteria require primary studies (RCTs or quasi-RCTs) with an inactive control arm, which this article does not meet. There is no description of participant recruitment, randomisation, or a direct comparison between PFMT and an inactive control. Therefore, the study clearly does not satisfy the design criterion.

This study is a descriptive anatomical and physiological paper on urethrovesical structure, not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. It does not enroll women with SUI, UUI, or MUI, does not include an arm with pelvic floor muscle training, and does not have a no-treatment or inactive control arm. Thus, it fails to meet the study design and population requirements of the selection criteria.

This study describes the development and validation of a self-report symptom inventory for psychiatric symptoms (anxiety, depression, etc.) and does not involve women with urinary incontinence, pelvic floor muscle training, or an inactive control arm. It is not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial and is entirely unrelated to the review's population, intervention, comparison, or outcome criteria.

The abstract is clearly not a primary randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trial. It describes a book chapter or overview narrative ('In this chapter, we cover studies that provide comparative data ...'), summarising multiple conservative management approaches (lifestyle modification, PFMT, biofeedback, etc.) for UI or POP. It does not report any new trial data, randomisation procedure, or specific comparison of PFMT versus an inactive control. The selection criteria require individual RCTs or quasi-RCTs in women with SUI, UUI or MUI, with one arm being PFMT and the other being no treatment, placebo, sham, or another inactive control. Because this is a summary chapter rather than a trial, it unequivocally fails to meet the study design requirement.

This study is a methodological paper discussing post-randomisation exclusions and the intention-to-treat principle. It is not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial, does not include women with stress, urgency, or mixed urinary incontinence, does not involve any intervention (PFMT or otherwise), and has no comparison between PFMT and an inactive control. It does not meet any of the eligibility criteria for this review.

The selection criteria require a control arm that is no treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control. The study title states 'versus other active treatments', indicating the comparator is an active treatment, not an inactive control. This directly fails the protocol's PICO-comparator criterion. Additionally, the abstract does not describe a randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trial and appears to be background information rather than a primary study. Therefore, the study clearly does not meet inclusion criteria.

The study is a methodological communication about outcome measures for urinary incontinence, not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial. It does not describe any comparison between PFMT and no treatment, placebo, sham or other inactive control treatment. Therefore, it does not meet the review's selection criteria.

The study is an observational cohort study nested within a quasi-experimental cohort study, not a randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trial as required by the criteria. It does not compare PFMT to a no treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control treatment arm; rather, it compares morphological/functional deficits between stress and mixed UI, with PFM exercises only mentioned as part of the larger study. Therefore, it fails both the study design and comparison criteria.

The study compares two active treatment arms: a conservative treatment group (physiotherapy and bladder retraining) versus a urodynamic-guided tailored treatment group. Neither arm is a no-treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control. The control arm is an active diagnostic and therapeutic pathway, thus failing the comparator criterion that requires one arm be an inactive control.

This is a cross-sectional observational study of the causes of urinary incontinence in institutionalized elderly. It does not involve any intervention, specifically no pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) arm, nor any control group. The study design is not a randomized or quasi-randomised controlled trial, and therefore does not meet the review's inclusion criteria which require such designs with a PFMT intervention versus a control condition.
